statement: Lina folds a sheet of paper in half three times in a row, then punches one hole through all the layers, away from the edges. How many holes are there when she unfolds it?

choices.misconception: I counted one hole for each fold.
I counted the layers as 1, 2 and 4, one number for each fold, but 1 layer is the flat sheet before any folding.
I thought three folds make 2 x 3 = 6 layers, but each fold doubles the layers, so they go 2, 4, 8.
I added the layers after each fold, 2 + 4 + 8, as if every fold left its own holes.

hints: Draw the paper after each fold and count the layers.
Draw the diagram: the punch goes through every layer, so the number of holes equals the number of layers. Sketch how one fold in half changes the number of layers.
One fold makes 2 layers. The next fold lays those 2 layers on top of 2 more.

solutions.reliable: Count the layers. Flat, the sheet is 1 layer. Each fold in half doubles the layers: 2 after the first fold, 4 after the second and 8 after the third. The punch makes one hole in every layer, so the unfolded sheet has 8 holes. Check by unfolding in your head: opening the last fold turns 1 hole into 2, the next turns 2 into 4, and the first turns 4 into 8. The transferable idea: draw each stage instead of guessing, and look for what doubles.
solutions.elegant: Work backwards from the folded paper: every unfolding doubles the holes, because each hole has a mirror image across the fold. Three unfoldings turn 1 hole into 2, then 4, then 8.

whyOnTest: Sketching each fold turns a hard-to-picture question into counting layers, so drawing the diagram is what stops the add-instead-of-double slip.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
